Above 15 reps these estimates get much less accurate — managing that many reps is a good sign you can try a heavier weight.

The Epley formula, published by strength coach Boyd Epley in 1985, is the most widely used one-rep-max estimator in training apps, spreadsheets, and gym folklore. It is a simple linear model: every rep you perform beyond the first adds one thirtieth of the bar weight to the estimate. That linearity makes it easy to reason about — double the extra reps and you double the added credit — and it behaves predictably across the whole rep range. Epley and Brzycki, the two most popular formulas, agree exactly at 10 reps; below 10 Epley is slightly more conservative than Brzycki, and above 10 it becomes the more generous of the two. Like all estimators it is most trustworthy when the set is taken close to failure with moderate reps, roughly 2 to 10, where the relationship between reps and load is close to linear for most lifters. Because it neither collapses at high reps nor exaggerates low-rep sets, it is a sensible default when you have no strong reason to prefer another model, which is exactly why so much software ships with it. LogTrain uses Epley as its default formula.

Matt Brzycki, a strength coach and author at Princeton University, published this formula in 1993 and it has since become the estimator most often cited in academic validation studies. Unlike Epley's straight line, Brzycki is hyperbolic: the estimate is the weight multiplied by 36 divided by (37 minus reps). Each additional rep therefore counts a little more than the one before it, and the curve accelerates as reps climb. In the low-rep range, up to about 10 reps, Brzycki tracks measured maxes closely and research generally rates it among the most accurate of the classic formulas there. Beyond 10 reps the denominator shrinks quickly and the estimate grows aggressively, so treat high-rep predictions with skepticism — a 20-rep set of a light weight will produce a flattering number that few lifters could actually lift for a single. Brzycki and Epley agree exactly at 10 reps, with Brzycki slightly higher below that point. Choose it if you usually test with heavy sets of 3 to 8 reps and want the estimator with the strongest research pedigree in that range. LogTrain clamps the rep count at 36 so the math stays finite.

The Lombardi formula takes a completely different mathematical shape from its linear and hyperbolic siblings: it multiplies the weight by the rep count raised to the power of 0.1. A power law with such a small exponent produces the gentlest curve of any common estimator — the estimate rises quickly over the first few reps and then flattens dramatically, so a 10-rep set is credited only about 26 percent above the bar weight and a 20-rep set barely more. That restraint is the whole point. Where Epley and especially Brzycki inflate high-rep sets into eye-catching maxes, Lombardi stays skeptical, which makes it the best fit for lifters who log endurance-style sets of 12, 15, or 20 reps and want a number they could plausibly hit on a heavy single. The trade-off is the mirror image: for genuinely heavy doubles and triples Lombardi gives the least credit of the four, so pure strength athletes testing at low reps may find it undersells them. Pick Lombardi if your training lives in the higher rep ranges and you would rather be pleasantly surprised at the bar than let down by it.

Published by O'Conner and colleagues in 1989, this formula is the cautious sibling of Epley. It uses the same linear idea — every rep beyond the first adds a fixed fraction of the bar weight — but the fraction is 1/40 instead of Epley's 1/30, so each rep earns 25 percent less credit. The result is a deliberately conservative estimate across the entire rep range: at 5 reps O'Conner predicts 12.5 percent over the bar weight where Epley predicts nearly 17 percent. That restraint is valuable in situations where overestimating a max is riskier than underestimating it. Coaches programming percentages for beginners often prefer it, because a novice's estimated max sets their working weights for weeks, and an inflated number bakes in loads they cannot recover from. It also suits older lifters, rehab settings, and anyone returning from a layoff, where a margin of safety matters more than bragging rights. Because it is linear, it remains stable and predictable at higher reps rather than accelerating like Brzycki. Choose O'Conner when you want your training numbers anchored to what you can almost certainly lift, not what you might lift on a perfect day.
Tap a formula or classification to make it the default wherever BMI is shown.

The standard body mass index divides weight in kilograms by height in meters squared. The Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet devised the ratio in the 1830s while searching for a simple description of the average man, and in the 1970s the physiologist Ancel Keys confirmed it as the best of the easy height-weight indexes and gave it its modern name. It is the formula behind virtually every BMI chart, medical guideline, and study you will encounter, so if you want a number that is directly comparable with what a doctor or a paper reports, this is the one to use. Its weaknesses are equally well documented. Squaring height flatters tall people and penalizes short ones slightly, because real bodies do not scale in only two dimensions. More importantly for lifters, it cannot tell muscle from fat: a muscular person can read as overweight while carrying very little fat. Treat it as a population screening tool rather than a verdict on an individual physique. LogTrain uses Standard as its default formula.

Nick Trefethen, professor of numerical analysis at the University of Oxford, proposed this revision in a 2013 letter to The Economist. His observation was that the standard index scales weight against height squared, as if people were two-dimensional, while true three-dimensional scaling would use height cubed; real bodies grow somewhere in between, because taller people are not simply scaled-up copies of shorter ones. He split the difference with an exponent of 2.5 and multiplied by 1.3 so that adults of average height get roughly the same number under either formula. The effect is a modest correction at the extremes: short people score a little higher than the standard index says, and tall people score a little lower — undoing the standard formula's tendency to flatter the tall and penalize the short. The values land on the same scale, so the usual category cutoffs still apply. The New BMI has not been adopted by any health body and remains a mathematician's refinement rather than a clinical standard, but it is a reasonable choice if you are notably tall or short and want a fairer number.

The World Health Organization's international classification is the one behind the familiar BMI chart: below 18.5 is underweight, 18.5 to just under 25 is the normal range, 25 to just under 30 is overweight, and 30 or above is obese. The bands trace back to actuarial and epidemiological work linking body mass to mortality, and the WHO formalized them for adults in the 1990s as simple, memorable action points where health risks begin to climb. Because nearly every study, guideline, and medical record uses these cutoffs, they are the right choice when you want your category to match what a clinician or published research would say. Their main caveat is that risk does not rise at the same BMI in every population: the thresholds were derived largely from European data, and for some groups disease risk climbs noticeably earlier — which is exactly what the Asian-Pacific classification addresses. The categories also inherit BMI's blindness to body composition, so a muscular lifter should read them loosely. LogTrain uses the WHO international classification by default.

In 2000 the WHO's Western Pacific regional office, with the International Obesity Task Force, published The Asia-Pacific Perspective: Redefining Obesity, proposing lower action points for adults of Asian descent: overweight from a BMI of 23 and obesity from 27.5, instead of the international 25 and 30. The evidence behind it is that at the same BMI, many Asian populations carry a higher percentage of body fat and face a higher risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, so waiting for the international thresholds means acting too late. A 2004 WHO expert consultation published in The Lancet endorsed 23 and 27.5 as public-health action points, and several countries, including India, Singapore, and Japan, use cutoffs in this range in clinical practice. The underweight boundary stays at 18.5, and the BMI number itself is unchanged — only the point where it starts counting as elevated moves down. Choose this classification if your background is South or East Asian, or if your clinician uses the lower action points with you.
